title: pprof CPU Profiling, Memory Allocation Profiling, Execution Tracer

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A factory wants to know why production is slow. Two tools: a stopwatch survey (CPU profile) that samples what each worker is doing every few moments — after an hour, the tally shows which stations eat the most time. A camera log (execution trace) records EVERY move in perfect order — every worker's start, pause, and handoff — so you can see the exact timeline, including who waited for whom. The survey is cheap and finds hot spots; the camera log is detailed but heavier to record and analyze.
progressiveExplaining.junior: Go profiling: import _ "net/http/pprof" and hit /debug/pprof/ endpoints. CPU profile: go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile (samples for 30s). Heap profile: .../debug/pprof/heap. Then analyze with go tool pprof: top, list, web. The execution tracer: go run -trace trace.out and analyze with go tool trace — shows goroutine scheduling, GC, and system events over time. CPU profiling answers 'where is CPU time spent'; heap profiling answers 'where are allocations coming from'; the tracer answers 'why is my program waiting/slow in time'. Use pprof for CPU/memory hot spots, trace for concurrency/scheduling problems.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, Go's CPU profiler is a SAMPLING profiler: the runtime interrupts each thread periodically (the SIGPROF signal at a default rate of 100 Hz, or 1ms), records the current program counter stack, and accumulates samples into a profile. The result is statistical — hot functions get proportionally more samples. The heap profile is sampled too (allocation profiling samples every N bytes by default) and reports both live and cumulative allocations. The execution tracer records ALL scheduling and runtime events (goroutine create/block/unblock, syscall, GC, timer) with timestamps and goroutine ids, enabling precise timeline analysis. pprof and trace serve different questions.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: The CPU profiler uses setitimer/SIGPROF: a signal handler captures the interrupted thread's stack (via runtime stack walking with PC values and symbolization). The pprof format is a protobuf with sample types (cpu, inuse_space, alloc_space). Heap profiling uses the allocator's sampling hooks: every N bytes allocated, a stack sample is recorded (with the number of bytes), and profiles can be 'inuse' (live) or 'alloc' (cumulative), and 'space' or 'objects'. The execution tracer uses the runtime's trace buffer: a lock-free per-P buffer of trace events flushed by a dedicated goroutine to the output; go tool trace parses it and renders goroutine states, heap/GC, and network blocking. This is why the tracer has higher overhead than CPU sampling.

interviewGotchas.question: Why is Go's CPU profiler a sampling profiler, and what are its limitations?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the profiling methodology — interviewers want the SIGPROF sampling mechanism, the statistical nature, and the blind spots (short-lived functions, I/O waits).
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: The CPU profiler interrupts each thread with SIGPROF at a fixed rate (default 100 Hz) and records the current stack. It's SAMPLING, not instrumenting every call: hot functions accumulate proportionally more samples, so after enough samples the distribution approximates where CPU time is spent. Limitations: very short-lived functions that complete between samples can be missed; functions called rarely but each expensive may be under-sampled; the profile reflects CPU time ON the thread, not wall-clock waits — a goroutine blocked on I/O or a channel produces no CPU samples, so a CPU profile will NOT show 'waiting' problems. For waits, use the execution tracer or block profiles. Also, sampling rate and duration matter: short profiles may not represent steady state.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'the profile shows everything the program did'. It samples CPU on-thread stacks; I/O waits and lock blocks are invisible in the CPU profile. Another trap: profiling for 1 second and trusting the distribution — run long enough (30s+) for statistical significance, and under realistic load. Candidates who describe the sampling mechanism and the CPU-vs-wait distinction show real understanding.

interviewGotchas.question: What is the difference between a CPU profile, a heap profile, and the execution tracer, and when do you use each?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests tool selection — interviewers want the question each tool answers and the overhead trade-off, which determines the right diagnostic for a symptom.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: A CPU profile answers 'where is CPU time spent?' — sampled stacks of on-thread execution; use it for CPU-bound hot spots (a function eating 80% of samples). A heap profile answers 'where do allocations come from?' — sampled allocation stacks, reported as live (inuse) or cumulative (alloc), by space or objects; use it for GC pressure, high allocation rates, or memory growth. The execution tracer answers 'why is the program slow in TIME?' — it records every scheduling event (goroutine lifecycle, syscalls, GC, timers) with timestamps, so you can see a goroutine blocked on a channel, a mutex convoy, GC spikes, or network waits that no CPU profile shows. Overhead: CPU/heap sampling is cheap; the tracer is heavier (records every event) and is meant for targeted analysis, not always-on production.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'the tracer replaces profiling'. They answer different questions — the tracer shows waits/scheduling, not CPU hot spots. Another trap: using the heap profile's default (inuse_space) when you need cumulative allocations to find allocation-rate problems — use -alloc_space. Candidates who map symptoms to tools show real diagnostic skill.
